beats.intro: Chapter eight. [[sub]]Equity is a claim on a company. This chapter covers the types of equity securities, and how equity creates value.
beats.history: Why hold equities? [[bars]]Over 1900 to 2017, world equities earned about five point two percent a year after inflation. Bonds earned two percent. Bills earned under one percent. [[grow]]Compounded, one unit invested in equities grew to roughly three hundred seventy seven times its original value, in real terms. In bonds, about ten times. In bills, about two and a half. [[note]]Equities carry more risk, and in return they have rewarded investors with a higher return over the long run.
beats.common: Common shares are an ownership interest. [[rights]]Holders have a claim on operating performance, through dividends and growth. They can take part in decisions by voting. And they have a claim on net assets if the company is liquidated, after creditors. [[stat]]With statutory voting, each share gets one vote for each open board seat. With one hundred shares and three seats, you can cast at most one hundred votes for each seat. [[cum]]With cumulative voting, you may put all three hundred votes on one nominee, which helps minority shareholders win a seat. [[call]]Some common shares are callable, so the issuer may buy them back at a set price. Others are putable, so the holder may sell them back.
beats.preference: Preference shares rank ahead of common shares for dividends and in liquidation. They usually carry no vote, and pay a fixed dividend. [[cum]]With cumulative preference shares, a missed dividend piles up, and must be paid before common holders get anything. Non-cumulative shares lose a missed dividend. [[part]]Participating preference shares also share in profits above a set level. Non-participating shares receive only their fixed amount. [[more]]They may also be convertible into common shares, callable by the issuer, or putable by the holder.
beats.private: Equity can also be private. [[feat]]Private equity is sold in private placements, mainly to institutions. It does not trade in secondary markets, so it is less liquid. [[vc]]Venture capital funds young companies. [[lbo]]A leveraged buyout takes over an established company, using a lot of debt. [[pipe]]A PIPE is a private investment in a public company's equity. [[goal]]The idea is to give management time to build value, and later take the company public.
beats.receipts: Depository receipts let investors hold foreign companies on their home exchange. [[flow]]A depository bank holds the foreign company's shares, and issues receipts against them. The receipts trade like ordinary shares. [[adr]]American depository receipts are denominated in US dollars, and trade on US markets. [[gdr]]Global depository receipts are similar, but carry restrictions on resale between investors. [[note]]They save investors from dealing with foreign exchanges and currencies directly.
beats.value: How does equity create value? [[roe]]Accounting return on equity is net income over average book equity. Say net income is one twenty, on a thousand of book equity: twelve percent. [[coe]]Cost of equity is the return shareholders require. Say nine percent. [[good]]Earning twelve against a nine percent requirement creates value, so the shares should be worth more than book value. [[bad]]Earning only eight percent destroys value, so the shares may be worth less than book. [[note]]Book value is an accounting number. Intrinsic value is the present value of future cash flows, and can only be estimated.
beats.wrap: Four things to keep. [[w1]]Over the long run, equities have earned higher real returns than bonds and bills. [[w2]]Common shares give ownership, votes and residual claims. Preference shares rank ahead, with fixed dividends. [[w3]]Private equity and depository receipts widen the ways to hold equity. [[w4]]Return on equity above the cost of equity creates value.
